title: File Paths & Globbing 🗂️
description: Work with absolute and relative paths, and use wildcards to match files like magic.

slides.title: Paths Revisited 🛤️
slides.content:
## Absolute vs Relative in Practice

- Absolute path: `/home/alice/Documents/report.txt` – works no matter where you are.
- Relative path: `Documents/report.txt` – only works if you are in `/home/alice`.

Use `..` to go up: `../../etc` from `/home/alice` goes to `/etc`.

**Tab completion** saves typing: press `Tab` to auto‑complete paths.

quizData.explanation: `..` goes up to `/home/alice`, then `Pictures` is a direct child.

slides.title: Globbing: Pattern Power 💥
slides.content:
## Wildcards for File Matching

Bash can expand special characters (**globs**) to match multiple filenames:

- `*` – any sequence of characters (including none)
- `?` – exactly one character
- `[abc]` – any one character inside the brackets
- `[a-z]` – any character in the range

Example: `ls *.txt` shows all files ending with `.txt`.

quizData.question: What glob pattern matches all files that start with 'a' and have exactly two characters? (e.g., ab, ac, a1)
quizData.explanation: `?` matches exactly one character. So `a?` matches 'a' followed by any single character.

slides.title: Globbing Tips 🧠
slides.content:
## Advanced Patterns

- `*.[ch]` matches files ending with `.c` or `.h`
- `[!a]` means NOT 'a' – any single character except 'a'.
- Globs are expanded **before** the command runs. So `ls *.jpg` becomes `ls photo1.jpg photo2.jpg`.

Be careful: if a pattern matches nothing, it might be passed literally (unless you set `nullglob`).

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Test Globs with echo
Before using a risky command like `rm`, test your glob: `echo *.tmp`. It shows exactly what files would be matched.
